extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of Aristotle's criteria and distinctions about self-control, pleasure, pain, and related moral states from Nicomachean Ethics (Books VII–VIII). Useful for philosophers, students, and instructors analyzing virtue theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control worse when from Lust than Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: "Imperfect Self-Control, arising from Lust, is more so than that arising from Anger: because in Anger there is no insolence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle judges the source of passion: self-control failures rooted in lust are more disgraceful than those rooted in anger because anger lacks insolence. Use the origin of the passion to assess relative blameworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter of Self-Control: bodily lusts and pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The object-matter of Self-Control and its imperfections are bodily Lusts and pleasures; some are proper to the human race and natural, others brutish, others from maimings or disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pleasures/lusts by origin (natural human, brutish, pathological). Only natural human pleasures are relevant to perfected self-mastery and utter absence of self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery and utter absence apply only to human-appropriate pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Only pleasures proper to the human race and natural both in kind and degree are the object-matter of Perfected Self-Mastery and utter absence of Self-Control; brutish or pathological pleasures are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing moral responsibility (perfected mastery or utter lack) for pleasures that are brutish or disease-caused; moral choice presupposes the proper human faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutishness vs Vice: absence vs corruption of highest principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutishness is not as low as Vice but is to be regarded with more fear: the highest principle is absent in brutes whereas corrupted in vicious humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate danger by whether the moral principle is absent (brutishness) or corrupted (vice); absence may be more fearful because it's not amendable by correcting a corrupted principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of dispositions regarding pleasures/pains (self-control taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: People may be disposed to yield to temptations most would resist (Imperfect Self-Control) or be superior to those to which most men yield (Self-Control); similarly for pains: Softness vs Endurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify agents according to how they respond to common temptations and pains; use these four labels to analyze moral character and relative standing among most men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control vs utter absence: motive and culpability distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of Imperfect Self-Control follows bodily pleasures in excess without acting on deliberate conviction; the man utterly destitute acts upon a conviction that following these pleasures is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral culpability by whether the agent has a settled conviction (utter absence) or merely yields without deliberation (imperfect). The former is harder to cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control who pursues excess for their own sake is incurable
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who pursues the excess of pleasant things for their own sake, and not for any resulting good, is utterly void of Self-Control and must be incapable of remorse and incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for motive (for its own sake) and absence of remorse as signs of incurable lack of self-control (confirmed vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding to violent/excessive temptations vs yielding to common ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Yielding to very violent and excessive pleasures or pains (where reasonable resistance was attempted) is forgivable; yielding to temptations which the common herd can resist is a matter for wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate blame when the temptation is unusually violent and resistance was attempted; increase blame when one fails against ordinary challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness and Luxury as failure-of-resistance character
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who is a slave to amusement or lets trivial inconveniences determine his behavior is commonly thought destitute of Self-Control but is really Soft; Luxury is a kind of Softness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between weakness of resistance to pains/troubles (softness) and moral failure to resist pleasures (imperfect self-control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two forms of Imperfect Self-Control: Precipitancy and Weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Weakness: having made resolutions but not abiding by them due to passion. Precipitancy: led by passion because one never formed resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose whether failures stem from lack of prior resolve (precipitancy) or from failing to uphold formed resolutions (weakness); temperament (sharp/melancholy) predisposes to precipitancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse distinguishes curable imperfect self-control from incurable vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The man utterly destitute of Self-Control is not given to remorse and is incurable; the man of Imperfect Self-Control is almost made up of remorse and may be cured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence and character of remorse as diagnostic for prognosis (curable vs incurable) and moral assessment (acute vs chronic disorder analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control vs Endurance: mastery vs resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Endurance consists in continued resistance but Self-Control in actual mastery; continued resistance and actual mastery differ as not being conquered is from conquering; Self-Control is more choiceworthy than Endurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize actual mastery (changing desires to conform to reason) over mere stoic resistance when evaluating moral excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperamental causes and comparative curability of imperfect forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Precipitance is common in those with sharp or melancholy temperaments (acting before Reason); weaknesses arising from habitual failure are easier to change than those due to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider constitutional temperament and habituation when predicting ease of moral improvement: habitual faults are easier than natural constitution to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Practical Wisdom (phronesis) to Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not possible for the same man to be both of Practical Wisdom and of Imperfect Self-Control because Practical Wisdom includes moral goodness and aptitude for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat practical wisdom as requiring moral character; cleverness alone does not imply practical wisdom and can coexist with imperfect self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive/stubborn persons vs genuinely self-controlled
rubrics_metrics.description: People who abide by their opinions (Positive) resemble self-controlled superficially, but differ: the man of Self-Control will be persuaded by Reason when occasion requires, whereas the Positive man resists persuasion even by Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish obstinate conviction from morally-grounded self-control; test willingness to change under reasons, not merely resistance to passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives matter: noble pleasures can justify departure from resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every person who departs from resolutions from pleasure is base; if the pleasure is noble (e.g., truthfulness perceived as noble), the departure may not indicate imperfect self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the nobility of the motivating pleasure and the agent's evaluative standpoint before condemning departures from prior resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of views on Pleasure and chief good
rubrics_metrics.description: Three current views: (1) no Pleasure is good; (2) some Pleasures are good but many are bad; (3) every Pleasure is good yet the Chief Good is not Pleasure. Various supporting arguments are listed for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether pleasure contributes to eudaimonia, weigh standard objections (pleasure as process, impediment to thought, pursued by children/brutes, not art-produced) against counterarguments (pleasure as active working, some pleasures are ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as active working of the natural state (not merely a process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure should be described as 'active working of the natural state, unimpeded,' not merely a sensible process of production; some pleasures are ends or active workings (e.g., contemplative acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize intellectual/contemplative pleasures as genuine, non-remedial pleasures that may count toward the Chief Good; do not reduce all pleasures to remedial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily pleasures: necessary vs excessive and their moral status
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily pleasures admit of excess and their excess produces low/bad character; necessary bodily pleasures may be good as 'not-bad' or up to a point, whereas excesses make one a low bad man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate bodily pleasures by necessity and degree; necessary pleasures in proper measure are acceptable, excesses indicate vice (utter lack or imperfection of self-control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures as remedies: violent pleasures pursued to drive out pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily Pleasure drives out Pain; people often pursue violent (strong) pleasures as remedies for excessive pain, which explains why bodily pleasures are frequently over-pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret some excessive pursuit of pleasure as compensatory for pain or chronic constitutional states (youth, melancholic temperament); consider underlying pain/remedy dynamics when assigning blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial (cure) pleasures vs naturally pleasant activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pleasures result as cures of deficiency and are not the same as pleasures that put a naturally pleasant part into action; remedial pleasures may be experienced as pleasant though they mask prior pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pleasures arising from cure (which may not be intrinsically choiceworthy) from pleasures that are natural expressions of a healthy state (which do not admit excess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and context matter for assessing pleasure/pain moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods and evils can be absolute or relative; some things may be bad absolutely but choiceworthy relatively (e.g., at certain times), so pleasures and pains must be evaluated in context, degree, and relation to the active working of states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid all-or-nothing judgments; consider context, duration, and whether the pleasure facilitates or hinders the unimpeded active working of a natural state.
